newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: No fuel price relief in sight for Asia airlines.
newsitem.headline: No fuel price relief in sight for Asia airlines.

text.p: Battered by rising fuel costs, Asian airlines are set for further pain in coming months as the fuel market enters its peak season during the northern winter, traders said on Wednesday.
High jet fuel prices are here to stay at least into the first quarter of 1997, they warned.

"Looking at the first quarter for the moment, (it's) pretty difficult to see prices below $30.00 (per barrel, free-on-board Singapore)," said Tom James, Asia Pacific regional manager for natural resources, at Credit Lyonnais Rouse Derivatives.
Echoing similar sentiments, a trader at a major oil company said: "Jet fuel prices are not likely to fall below $30.00 per barrel until after winter."
"If you look at the seasonal pattern (prices) should strengthen further," he said.
Singapore jet fuel prices have averaged around $30.00 per barrel since late August, compared with an average price of $22.80 in 1995.

And judging by energy derivative prices, which indicate what buyers and sellers believe prices will be in the future, the market expect prices to remain high. Swap derivatives show prices around $31.00 in December and January.
In the cash marekt, jet fuel for prompt delivery closed on Tuesday at $30.45 per barrel fob Singapore.
Traders noted jet fuel prices peak during the fourth quarter and first quarter of each year because the fuel is also used for heating during the northern hemisphere winter.
In January 1996, jet fuel prices soared to a five-year peak of almost $34.00 per barrel fob Singapore.
Regional demand for jet fuel is expected to be strong in coming weeks, market players believe, buoyed by the recent return of Japan, Indonesia and India to the market.
However, one factor which could take the steam out of strong jet fuel markets is a fall in crude oil prices, they said, though this was seen as unlikely due to strong demand for crude.
Japan, the region's largest winter consumer of jet/kerosene, bought four 240,000- barrel cargoes for November arrival to top up supplies from domestic refineries.

Japanese spot purchases for arrival in December and January may surpass a million barrels for each month if the winter is colder than expected, traders said. But they added the buying is not expected to match last year's magnitude because Japan has been building stocks.
"We won't see Japan rushing to buy until (the first quarter of next year) if the weather is cold," James said.

Japan's jet/kerosene stocks at the end of September totalled 4.76 million kilolitres, up 8.7 percent from a year ago and almost double the record low of 2.65 million kl in January which led to a surge in Japanese fuel imports.

India, another major regional consumer, is expected to buy more cargoes in December than November, market players said. In November, India bought only one 360,000-barrel cargo but is likely to buy four or five cargoes in December of the same size, they said.

IATA said the meeting of its 250 member airlines would consider "concerted action" to counter rising fuel costs.
The IATA said fuel prices paid by members were, on average, 13 percent higher in the first nine months of 1996 at 73.9 cents per U.S. gallon, compared with the same period a year ago.
